CORRECTIONS_AGAINST_THE_ORCHESTRATOR_BLO.14_three_one_shot_greps_produced_false_n: FT-079's stale clause (window too narrow), W4's proposed clause (anchored on a phrase that wraps across two lines), and the 33058734 dossier item (quoted phrase reconstructed from a verifier's rendering). Each time the text WAS there. A single failed exact-phrase grep is evidence about my pattern, never about the corpus.
CORRECTIONS_AGAINST_THE_ORCHESTRATOR_BLO.15_a_badly_posed_test_simulated_a_defect: My post-edit check asserted the ABSENCE of the string 'direzione solida' from line 122 — but the replacement text I had just written REINTRODUCES that phrase deliberately, as a quotation inside the dated note recording its withdrawal. So the check printed False and for two minutes I believed I had repeated the neighbour-check failure inside the very commit that denounced it. The predicate was wrong, not the file: the criterion is not 'the string is gone' but 'the string is no longer ASSERTED'. Verified by splitting line 122 at its correction note: the assertive part carries neither withdrawn phrase, and the file holds exactly one occurrence, which is the citation. This is the inverse of the familiar failure — here a badly built test SIMULATED a defect, where the usual danger is a green test HIDING one. Both are failures of the test, and neither is evidence about the corpus.
CORRECTIONS_AGAINST_THE_ORCHESTRATOR_BLO.16_I_chose_the_less_safe_of_two_offered_: ALDAZ-REEXAM-B-20260913 offered TWO wordings for DL-MECH-012's opening. I took 'sotto stimolo meccanico o in sistema cell-autonomo' — a FILTER, which excludes two of the three legs the same sentence then enumerates: the cerebellar leg has no imposed stimulus, and the sepsis leg is infective and whole-animal. The other offered wording, 'nei tessuti e sotto gli stimoli qui elencati', ENUMERATES instead of filtering and therefore excludes nothing. ALDAZ-REEXAM-B2-20260914 caught it as NARROWER_THAN_CLAIMED — the undershoot its own contract had named as the more dangerous failure — and stated plainly that the safer of the two offered wordings was the one not chosen. Fixed at f3eb7d5. The lesson is narrow and practical: when a verifier offers alternatives, the difference between them is usually the finding, and a filter and an enumeration are not interchangeable even when both are true of the head clause.
CORRECTIONS_AGAINST_THE_ORCHESTRATOR_BLO.17_stray_non_latin_characters_entered_a_: Drafting the blind R4 brief I emitted the two Han characters for 'background' inside an instruction to an actor: 'mean/<han>background</han> deficit'. This is a REPEAT of a class that already occurred in this mandate, when a Japanese fragment ('registry' + two kana) landed in a disposition table and had to be removed after reading the real line. The brief was already dispatched and a dispatched brief cannot be edited, so the defect stands in that actor's instructions; it is low-consequence there (the surrounding clause names the measurement in English twice) but it is not zero, because an instruction is where an ambiguity costs most. THE COUNTERMEASURE THAT WORKED, and it is the part worth keeping: before committing the §21d packet I ran a repertoire scan over the file and gated the commit on it, so the packet was verified clean (7418 bytes, no character outside the expected repertoire) BEFORE it landed rather than after. The lesson is asymmetric: I cannot retro-fix a brief, so the scan belongs before every write I commit, and a dispatched brief should be scanned before dispatch, not after.
